 The latest selloff in a high-flying chip stock shows just how demanding investors in the AI trade have become.
 Shares of Japanese memory-chip maker Kioxia closed 16% lower on Monday after a disappointing earnings outlook, despite continued strong demand for chips used in artificial intelligence infrastructure.
 Kioxia was among the biggest stock-market winners of the AI infrastructure boom, with its shares surging more than 750% in the first half of the year as investors bet on rising demand for data-center storage.
 Its September-quarter results were broadly in line with expectations, but its December-quarter revenue forecast and projected operating profit both missed consensus.
 The company's forecast for essentially flat quarterly revenue and profit was "a massive miss," Bernstein analysts led by Mark Li wrote in an October 30 note.
 Kioxia said its weaker outlook partly reflected delays in shipping data-center storage products, pushing some expected sales into the following quarter.
 A greater share of lower-priced products for smartphones and PCs is also expected to weigh on average selling price growth.
 Still, Kioxia expects memory supplies to remain tight in 2027, with its planned capacity for that year already sold out. Long-term agreements cover more than half its expected shipment volume in 2028.
 The selloff weighed on Japanese stocks, with the benchmark Nikkei 225 falling as much as 1% on Monday before recovering to end 0.3% lower.

 The declines followed a bruising week for US technology stocks, as investors scrutinized the enormous costs of AI development and how quickly companies can turn that spending into profits.
 The selloff came despite a broader boom in memory chips, which helped South Korea's Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix report record quarterly profits last week.
 SK Hynix offered greater visibility into future demand, with long-term customer agreements covering more than half its production capacity for 2027 and 2028. Its shares rallied following the earnings report.
